questions.question: Which of the following major incidents occurred in 1919?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following major incidents occurred in 1919?
questions.solution: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre took place on 13 April 1919 (on the day of Baisakhi). It took place at Jallianwala Bagh near the Golden Temple in Amritsar, Punjab province of India.A large peaceful crowd had gathered to protest against the Rowlatt Act.

questions.question: Which of the following was a major event of the year 1919?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following was a major event of the year 1919?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is the Passing of the Rowlatt Act.

  • The passing of the Rowlatt Act was a major event of the year 1919.

Key Points

  • ​​Rowlatt Act (1919):
    • It was passed during the time of Lord Chelmsford.
    • In 1919 a Sedition Committee headed by justice Rowlatt led to the Rowlatt Act.
    • It was passed during the time of Lord Chelmsford.
    • ​​Rowlatt Act authorized the government to imprison any person without trial and conviction by the Court of Law for 2 years.
    • The law also enabled the government to suspend the right of Habeas Corpus which had been the foundation of civil liberties in Britain.
    • To protest the arrest of Dr. Saifuddin Kitchlu and Dr. Satyapal many people gathered at Jallianwala Bagh and General Reginald Dyer ordered indiscriminate heavy firing on them which led to the Jallianwala Bagh Massacre (13th April 1919 AD).
    • Mahatma Gandhi returned the Kaisar-i-Hind title as a protest against the Jallianwala Bagh massacre.
    • Rabindranath Tagore returned ‘Knighthood’.

Additional Information

  • The Formation of the Swaraj Party took place in the year 1923.
  • Gandhi-Irwin Pact was signed on 5th March 1931 AD.
  • The Launch of the Non-Cooperation Movement took place in 1920.

questions.question: Who among the following persons can be described as 'a spokesperson of the backward classes and castes in India'?
questions.questionHtml: Who among the following persons can be described as 'a spokesperson of the backward classes and castes in India'?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar.Key Points

  • Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar can be described as 'a spokesperson of the backward classes and castes in India'.
  • Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar did a valuable work of creating awareness in the untouchable society.
  • He was born in Mahu, a village near Indore in Madhya Pradesh.
  • Due to his work, the people and activists awarded him the title of Babasaheb.
  • Babasaheb did the work of social awareness and organization of Dalits.
  • On 20 July 1924, he established the Bhiskrit Hitkarani Sabha.
  • In 1927, Babasaheb organized the Mahad Satyagraha to see the Chavdar Thalai at Mahad to give courage and confidence to the untouchables.
  • Babasaheb started a newspaper to educate the Dalits and the main papers were Mooknayak, Bahishkrit Bharat, and Janata.
  • He embraced Buddhism on 14 October 1956 at Nagpur.

Additional Information

  • Sardar Patel was born on 31st October 1875 in Nadiad, Gujarat.
    • He was the first Home Minister and Deputy Prime Minister of India.
    • He played an important role in the integration of many Indian princely states to make an Indian federation.
    • At the time of independence, Sardar Patel played a key role in convincing several princely states to align with the Indian Union.
    • He also worked hard as a social leader for the Independence of India.
    • Women of Bardoli bestowed the title ‘Sardar’ on Vallabhbhai Patel, which means ‘a Chief or a Leader’.
  • Dr. Rajendra Prasad was the longest-serving President of India (1950 to 1962).
    • Dr. Rajendra Prasad was elected as the first President of India on 24th January 1950
    • He was one of the prominent leaders of the Indian independence movement and played a prominent role as the President of the Indian National Congress. 
    • He served as the president of the Constituent Assembly that drafted the first constitution of the Republic of India, which lasted from 1948 to 1950.
  • ​Subhas Chandra Bose was born on 23rd January 1897 in Cuttack, Orissa.
    • One of the greatest freedom fighters of India popularly known as Netaji.
    • Subhas Chandra Bose was elected twice as the president of the INC in the Haripura session in 1938 and the Tripuri session in 1939.
    • Subhas Chandra Bose founded the All India Forward Bloc on 22nd June 1939.

questions.question: When was Rowlatt Satyagraha launched and by whom?
questions.questionHtml: When was Rowlatt Satyagraha launched and by whom?
questions.solution: Rowlatt Satyagraha was a nationwide satyagraha against the proposed Rowlatt Act (1919). It was launched by Mahatma Gandhi in 1919.

questions.question: In which year was the Rowlatt Act passed in India?
questions.questionHtml: In which year was the Rowlatt Act passed in India?
questions.solution: The Rowlatt Act, officially known as the "Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act of 1919," was enacted in 1919 by the Imperial Legislative Council. It was based on the recommendations of the Rowlatt Commission of 1918, led by Sir Sydney Rowlatt. The act aimed to replace the temporary wartime provisions of the Defence of India Act 1915 with a permanent law to curb the growing unrest among Indians. It severely restricted civil liberties, including the right to liberty and expression. Mahatma Gandhi called it the Black Act, and it was eventually repealed in 1922.

questions.question: Mahatma Gandhi called off the Non-cooperation Movement in February 1922 after which incident?
questions.questionHtml: Mahatma Gandhi called off the Non-cooperation Movement in February 1922 after which incident?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Chauri Chaura Incident

Key Points

  • Chauri Chaura incident:-
    • On February 5, 1922, a mob of protesters participating in the Non-cooperation Movement at Chauri Chaura in Uttar Pradesh, India, clashed with the police.
    • The protesters set fire to the police station, killing 22 policemen.
    • Mahatma Gandhi called off the Non-cooperation Movement in February 1922 after the Chauri Chaura incident. (Hence option 1 is correct)

Additional Information

  • Jallianwala Bagh massacre:-
    • It was also known as the Amritsar massacre, took place on April 13, 1919, in Jallianwala Bagh, Amritsar, Punjab, British India. 
  • Kakori train robbery:-
    • It was an armed robbery that took place on August 9, 1925, on a train in central Uttar Pradesh, India.
    • It was organized by the Indian revolutionaries of Hindustan Republican Association (HRA).
  • Bomb Blast in central assembly:-
    • On April 8, 1929, a bomb exploded in the Central Legislative Assembly in Delhi, India.
    • The bomb was thrown by Bhagat Singh, a member of the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA).
    • The bomb blast was intended to protest against the British rule in India.

questions.question: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi returned to India in the year ______ after two decades of residence abroad.
questions.questionHtml: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi returned to India in the year ______ after two decades of residence abroad.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 1915.

Important Points

  • Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi landed on January 9, 1915, at the Apollo Bunder in Bombay after two decades of residence abroad.
  • He received a "Kaiser-i-Hind" gold medal in the King’s birthday honors list of 1915.
  • His political mentor on the Indian scene was Gopal Krishna Gokhale.
  • Lord Hardinge’s open support of the Satyagraha movement had in any case removed the stigma of rebellion from South Africa’s Indian movement.

Key Points

  • As a 19-year-old, Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi had left India for the first time on September 4, 1888, to get enrolled in the centuries-old law institute Inner Temple in London.
  • In 1894 Gandhi tried his first criminal cases in South Africa.
  • From 1893 till 1913 Gandhiji practiced in South Africa.
  • On March 12, 1930, Indian independence leader Mohandas Gandhi begins a defiant march to the sea in protest of the British salt monopoly.
  • Gandhi set out from Sabarmati Ashram, Ahmadabad with 78 followers on a 241-mile march to the coastal town of Dandi on the Arabian Sea.
    • They reached Dandi on April 5, Gandhi was at the head of a crowd of tens of thousands. Gandhi spoke and led prayers and early the next morning walked down to the sea to make salt.

questions.question: Which of the following pacts suspended the Civil Disobedience Movement?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following pacts suspended the Civil Disobedience Movement?
questions.solution: The Gandhi-Irwin Pact, signed on 5 March 1931 between Mahatma Gandhi and Lord Irwin, suspended the Civil Disobedience Movement. Congress agreed to attend the Second Round Table Conference and cease the movement, while the British released non-violent political prisoners and returned confiscated properties.

questions.question: Who among the following along with Motilal Nehru was instrumental in the creation of the Swaraj Party?

The correct answer is Chittaranjan Das.

questions.question: In which of the following years was the Second Round Table Conference in London held?
questions.questionHtml: In which of the following years was the Second Round Table Conference in London held?
questions.solution:
• The Second Round Table Conference was held in London in 1931.

  • Gandhiji participated in the Second Round Table Conference.
  • Gandhi-Irwin Pact is associated with the Second Round Table Conference.

questions.question: In which of the following years was the Gandhi-Irwin Pact signed?
questions.questionHtml: In which of the following years was the Gandhi-Irwin Pact signed?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 1931.Key Points

  • The Gandhi-Irwin pact was signed in 1931.
  • The Gandhi-Irwin pact was signed between Mahatma Gandhi and the then Viceroy of India, Lord Irwin on March 5, 1931.
  • The features of the Gandhi-Irwin pact:
    • Congress would participate in the Second Round Table Conference.
    • Congress would discontinue the Civil Disobedience Movement.
    • The Government would withdraw all ordinances issued to curb Congress.
    • The Government would withdraw all prosecutions relating to offenses other than violent ones.
    • The Government would release all persons undergoing sentences of imprisonment for their activities in the civil disobedience movement.

Additional Information 

  • Civil Disobedience Movement
    • The Civil Disobedience Movement was started by Gandhi on 12th March 1930 with his famous Dandi March. 
    • Together with 78 chosen followers, Gandhi walked nearly 375 km from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi, a village on the Gujarat sea coast.
    • On the morning of 6th April 1930, Gandhiji broke the salt law by making salt. Thousands of people followed suit.
    • This movement resulted in Gandhi-Irwin Pact on 5 March 1931.
    • Indians were allowed to make salt for domestic use.
    • Gandhiji attended the Second Round Table Conference in London as an ‘equal’.

questions.question: Due to which of the following events did Rabindranath Tagore return the title of 'Knighthood' to the British Government while expressing his anguish?
questions.questionHtml: Due to which of the following events did Rabindranath Tagore return the title of 'Knighthood' to the British Government while expressing his anguish?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Jallianwala Bagh massacre.

Key Points

  • ​​​​​​The Amritsar Massacre, also known as the Jallianwala Bagh Massacre, happened on April 13, 1919. At the Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar, Punjab, a sizable peaceful crowd had gathered to protest the Rowlatt Act and the detention of pro-independence activists Saifuddin Kitchlew and Satyapal. 
  • In opposition to the mass murder in Jalianwalla Bagh, Tagore surrendered his knighthood. Rabindranath Tagore's letter to Lord Chelmsford, the British viceroy, in which he revoked his knighthood in opposition to the mass murder at Jalianwalla Bagh.
  • The Nobel laureate was given a moving account of the slaughter by Ruchi Ram Sahni, a former Trustee of The Tribune, which led Tagore to decline the knighthood. In 1915, two years after winning the Nobel Prize for Literature, Rabindranath Tagore was made a knight.
  • The term "knight" might be applied to positions of higher aristocracy, such as landowners, despite the fact that it was mainly a title for a military function. In exchange for the vassals' fidelity, defence, and service, the higher nobles grant them their fiefs, or parcels of land. 

Additional Information

  • ​​​On 14 January 1931, on the day of Makar Sankranti, the British military force surrounded and open gunfires on the public present in the peaceful public meeting of freedom fighters at Singhpur Charanpaduka Maidan located on the banks of Urmila river in Chhatarpur district Madhya Pradesh. Charan Paduka Massacre has been called as the Jallianwala Bagh massacre of Madhya Pradesh.
  • The Partition of Bengal was announced on 19 July 1905 by the then Viceroy Lord Curzon. It was implemented on 16 October 1905. However, in 1911 it was withdrawn by Lord Hardinge. The stated reason was to ease the administration. But the actual reason was to weaken the growing nationalism in Bengal and break the unity.
  • The Chauri Chaura incident took place in British India on February 4, 1922, at Chauri Chaura in the Gorakhpur district of the United Province (modern Uttar Pradesh), when a sizable crowd of demonstrators taking part in the Non-cooperation movement battled with police, who then opened fire.

questions.questionHtml: Who among the following signed the Poona pact with Mahatma Gandhi?
questions.solution: Bhimrao Ambedkar signed the Poona pact with Mahatma Gandhi in 1932. The Poona pact was an agreement between the leaders of the Dalit community and the Indian National Congress, which aimed to secure reserved seats for Dalits in the provincial legislative councils.

questions.question: In 1932, the Poona Pact was signed between Mahatma Gandhi and _________.
questions.questionHtml: In 1932, the Poona Pact was signed between Mahatma Gandhi and _________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar.

Key Points

  • Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar, an eminent Indian jurist, economist, politician, and social reformer, played a key role in the anti-caste movement in India.
  • The Poona Pact was an agreement between Mahatma Gandhi and Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar on behalf of the depressed classes (now known as Scheduled Castes).
  • The pact was signed on 24th September 1932 in Yerwada Central Jail, Pune.
  • It aimed at providing reserved seats for the depressed classes in the provincial legislatures within the general electorate.

Additional Information

  • Background of the Poona Pact:
    • Prior to the Poona Pact, the British government had announced the Communal Award in 1932, which provided separate electorates for minorities and the depressed classes.
    • Dr. Ambedkar supported the separate electorates as it would provide political representation to the oppressed classes.
    • Mahatma Gandhi opposed the separate electorates, fearing it would divide Hindu society.
    • He went on a hunger strike to protest against it, leading to negotiations between Gandhi and Ambedkar.
  • Terms of the Poona Pact:
    • The Poona Pact provided for a single Hindu electorate, with reserved seats for the depressed classes.
    • Out of the total 148 seats in the provincial legislatures, 71 seats were reserved for the depressed classes.
    • Additionally, the pact ensured adequate representation of the depressed classes in the central legislature and other sectors.
  • Significance of the Poona Pact:
    • The pact marked a significant moment in the history of India's struggle for independence, reflecting the internal challenges of caste and social inequality.
    • It highlighted the efforts to integrate the depressed classes into the mainstream political framework of India.
    • The agreement paved the way for future affirmative action policies in India aimed at the upliftment of marginalized communities.

questions.question: The objective of Simon Commission was to ______.

questions.question: The Poona Pact of 1932 was an agreement between Mahatma Gandhi and ______.
questions.questionHtml: The Poona Pact of 1932 was an agreement between Mahatma Gandhi and ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is BR Ambedkar.

Key Points

  • On 24 September 1932, the Poona Pact was sealed between Mahatma Gandhi and Dr. B R Ambedkar in the Yerwada Central Jail, Pune. 
  • Gandhiji was undertaking a fast against the British government’s decision to grant separate electorates for the ‘Depressed classes’.
  • The separate electorate for Dalits was a topic upon which Gandhi and Ambedkar could not agree.
  • In the First Round Table Conference held in 1930, Dr. Ambedkar had demanded a separate electorate for the ‘Depressed classes’ whom he was representing.
  • Gandhi and the Congress Party were against the idea of separate electorates for any class as it was seen as a means to weaken and divide Indian society.
  • The then British Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald granted the ‘Communal Award’ to minority communities including the ‘Depressed classes’.
  • Gandhi protested against this award (also known as the MacDonald Award) by undertaking a fast unto death whilst in jail in Poona.
  • When Gandhi started his fast, there was public pressure on Ambedkar to step in and stop the fast. This resulted in the Poona Pact.​

Additional Information

  • Provisions of the Poona Pact
    • Seats would be reserved for the ‘Depressed classes’ in the Provincial Councils.
    • The number of seats reserved for the provinces depended on the strength of the provinces:
      • Madras: 30; Punjab: 8; Bombay and Sindh: 15; Central Provinces: 20; Bihar and Orissa: 18; Bengal: 30; United Provinces: 20; and Assam: 7 (Total reserved: 148)
    • In the Central Legislature, 19% of the seats would be reserved for the Depressed Classes.
    • The members of the depressed classes who were eligible to vote would form an electoral college. This College would elect four candidates among the depressed classes on the basis of a single vote.
    • This principle of ‘Joint electorate and reserved seats’ was to be followed in the Central Assembly too.
    • It was agreed that this system would continue for ten years unless it was ended by mutual consent sooner.
    • It was also agreed upon to allocate a certain portion of money from the educational grant for the education of the depressed classes in all the provinces.
    • Nobody would be discriminated against because they belonged to the depressed classes in the matter of election to the local bodies or appointment to government service.

  • The final draft of the Indian Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949
  • The Constitution of India came into force on 26 January 1950.

questions.question: Bhagat Singh and ________ threw a bomb in the Central Legislative Assembly on 8 April 1929.
questions.questionHtml: Bhagat Singh and ________ threw a bomb in the Central Legislative Assembly on 8 April 1929.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Batukeshwar Dutt.

Key Points

  • Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt threw bombs in the Central Legislative Assembly on 8 April 1929 to protest against the repressive Public Safety Bill and Trade Disputes Bill.
  • The intent of the bombing was not to cause harm but to make the "deaf" British rulers hear India's demand for freedom.
  • They shouted slogans like "Inquilab Zindabad" (Long live the revolution) and threw pamphlets outlining their cause.
  • Both Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt voluntarily surrendered to the police after the bombing and were arrested on the spot.
  • This event gained significant attention and brought the Indian independence movement to the global stage.

Additional Information

  • Bhagat Singh: A revolutionary socialist, Bhagat Singh is considered one of the most influential freedom fighters in India's struggle for independence. He was known for his radical approach and sacrifice for the nation.
  • Batukeshwar Dutt: A close associate of Bhagat Singh, Batukeshwar Dutt was a revolutionary freedom fighter who participated in many activities against British rule, including the Assembly bombing.
  • Central Legislative Assembly Bombing: This act was a symbolic protest against British oppression and aimed to spark awareness among Indians about the need for independence.
  • Repressive Bills: The Public Safety Bill and Trade Disputes Bill were introduced by the British to curb civil liberties and workers' rights in India, which led to widespread dissent among Indians.
  • Outcome: Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt’s actions inspired the youth of India and became a rallying point for the independence movement. They were later tried and convicted for their roles in revolutionary activities.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is 1915 – Mahatma Gandhi returned from South Africa.

Key Points

  • After over 21 years of stay in South Africa, Gandhi returned to India on January 9, 1915, with his wife Kasturba.
  • He had been in London the previous year to treat a severe bout of pleurisy, a lung inflammation.
  • His doctors advised him to return to India to escape the English winter.
  • A hero's welcome awaited Gandhi when he landed on January 9, 1915, at the Apollo Bunder in Bombay. 
  • On 4 February 1916, Gandhiji made his first public appearance after returning from South Africa to BHU. He addressed the audience in BHU.
  • Pravasi Bharatiya Divas is a celebratory day observed on 9 January by the Republic of India to commemorate the return of Mahatma Gandhi from South Africa to Mumbai on 9 January 1915.

Additional Information

  • 1942 – The Cripps Mission was sent by the British government to India to obtain Indian cooperation for the British war efforts in the 2nd World War.
  • 1930 – The first Round Table Conference convened from 12 November 1930 to 19 January 1931.
  • 1942 – From 7 to 8 August 1942, The All India Congress Committee met in Bombay and ratified the 'Quit India' resolution.

questions.question: In which of the following years was the Gandhi-Irwin Pact signed with the government agreeing to release all political prisoners?
questions.questionHtml: In which of the following years was the Gandhi-Irwin Pact signed with the government agreeing to release all political prisoners?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 1931.

Key Points

  • The Gandhi-Irwin Pact was signed on March 5, 1931.
  • This pact was an agreement between Mahatma Gandhi and the then Viceroy of India, Lord Irwin.
  • The pact marked the end of the Civil Disobedience Movement in India.
  • As per the agreement, the British government agreed to release all political prisoners who had not committed violence.
  • Gandhi agreed to attend the Second Round Table Conference in London as a representative of the Indian National Congress.

Additional Information

  • Civil Disobedience Movement
    • Launched by Mahatma Gandhi in 1930 to protest against the British rule in India.
    • Included acts of non-violent resistance and non-cooperation with the British authorities.
  • Round Table Conferences
    • Series of three conferences held in London to discuss constitutional reforms in India.
    • Gandhi attended the Second Round Table Conference as part of the Gandhi-Irwin Pact.
  • Lord Irwin
    • He was the Viceroy of India from 1926 to 1931.
    • Played a significant role in negotiating with Indian leaders during the freedom struggle.

questions.question: The deliberations of the representatives at the Third Round Table Conference was held during the later months of which year?
questions.questionHtml: The deliberations of the representatives at the Third Round Table Conference was held during the later months of which year?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 1932.

Key Points

  • Third Round Table Conference:-
    • It was a series of meetings held in London from November 17, 1932, to December 24, 1932, to discuss the future of British India.
    • The conference was attended by representatives of the British government, Indian princes, and various political parties, including the Indian National Congress (INC).
    • However, the INC, led by Mahatma Gandhi, ultimately boycotted the conference due to disagreements with the British government over the scope of reforms and the representation of minority groups.
    • Despite the absence of the INC, the Third Round Table Conference made some significant progress towards Indian self-government.
    • The conference agreed to establish a federal system of government for India, with a central government and provincial legislatures.
    • It also agreed to expand the franchise and introduce measures to protect minority groups.
    • However, the conference failed to reach an agreement on the composition of the central legislature, which remained a major stumbling block to further constitutional reforms. 

Additional Information

  • First Round Table Conference:-
    • The First Round Table Conference was held in London in three sessions between November 1930 and January 1931.
    • The conference was attended by representatives of the British government, Indian princes, and various political parties, but the Indian National Congress (INC) did not participate.
    • The conference discussed a range of issues related to the future of British India, including dominion status, provincial autonomy, and minority rights.
    • The conference did not reach any major agreements, but it did help to establish a framework for further discussions.
  • Second Round Table Conference:-
    • The Second Round Table Conference was held in London in two sessions between September and December 1931.
    • The conference was attended by representatives of the British government, Indian princes, and various political parties, including the INC.
    • The INC participated in the conference after the British government agreed to release Gandhi from prison and suspend the Civil Disobedience Movement.
    • The conference discussed a range of issues related to the future of British India, including dominion status, provincial autonomy, and minority rights.
    • The conference reached some agreements on these issues, but it did not resolve all of the outstanding issues.

questions.question: Who were the prime accused in the Assembly bomb case that took place in 1929, Delhi?
questions.questionHtml: Who were the prime accused in the Assembly bomb case that took place in 1929, Delhi?
questions.solution: Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt were the prime accused in the Assembly bomb case that took place in 1929 Delhi. They were members of the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA). The incident occurred on April 8, 1929, when they threw two bombs into the Central Legislative Assembly as a protest against the Public Safety Bill and the Trade Dispute Act.

questions.question: Which of the following events took place in the United Provinces in February, 1922?
questions.questionHtml: Which of the following events took place in the United Provinces in February, 1922?
questions.solution: The Chauri Chaura incident occurred on February 4, 1922, in the United Provinces (now Uttar Pradesh), specifically in Chauri Chaura, a small town in the Gorakhpur district. This event was a violent clash between Indian protesters and British police during the Non-cooperation movement, resulting in the police station being set on fire and several police officials being killed. Consequently, many people were arrested. Following this incident, Mahatma Gandhi called off the Non-Cooperation Movement on February 12, 1922. This event marked a pivotal moment in the Indian independence movement.

questions.question: Who founded the Swaraj Party?
questions.questionHtml: Who founded the Swaraj Party?

options.text: Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Lala Lajpat Rai
options.html: Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Lala Lajpat Rai

questions.solution: The Swaraj Party was founded by C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru in 1923 within the Congress to advocate for a return to council politics. The party demanded the framing of a constitution for India and held its first session in Allahabad. It gained significant influence by securing over 40 seats in the 1923 central legislative assembly elections. C.R. Das served as the first president and Motilal Nehru as the first secretary. The party's influence waned after C.R. Das's death in 1925. Additionally, prominent leaders associated with other organizations include Lala Lajpat Rai (Punjab National Bank) and Mahatma Gandhi (Harijan Sevak Sangh).

questions.question: Who along with Bhagat Singh threw a bomb in the Legislative Assembly in April 1929?
questions.questionHtml: Who along with Bhagat Singh threw a bomb in the Legislative Assembly in April 1929?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Batukeshwar Dutta.

Key Points

  • On April 8, 1929, Bhagat Singh, along with freedom fighter Batukeshwar Dutt, hurled two bombs inside the Central Legislative Assembly in New Delhi to protest against an unfavorable Bill.
  • Bhagat Singh was a socialist revolutionary and freedom fighter who was executed at the age of 23 for his dramatic violence against British rule.
  • The famous slogan ‘Inquilab Zindabad’ was coined by him.
  • He was sentenced to death for the Lahore conspiracy case.

Additional Information

Sukhdev
  • He was a member of the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association.
Jatin Das
  • He was a bomb-maker of the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association from Bengal.
  • He was arrested by the British on 14 June 1929 for the Lahore Conspiracy Case.
  • He passed away in prison after a 63-day hunger strike.
Ajay Ghosh
  • He was an Indian freedom fighter and prominent leader of the Communist Party of India.
  • He was a member of the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association.
  • He was arrested and later imprisoned after the Lahore Conspiracy Case trial in 1929 but released after some time.
  • He was leading the Communist Party of India during the China-India war in 1962.

questions.question: Which revolutionary organisation was established at Feroz Shah Kotla in New Delhi in 1928?
questions.questionHtml: Which revolutionary organisation was established at Feroz Shah Kotla in New Delhi in 1928?
questions.solution: The Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA) was established in September 1928 at a meeting in the ruins of Feroz Shah Kotla, New Delhi. It evolved from the Hindustan Republic Association under the leadership of Chandra Shekhar Azad. The organization included prominent revolutionaries like Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev, and others, and aimed to adopt socialism as its official goal.

questions.question: In which prison did Mahatma Gandhi go on a hunger strike in protest of the British Government's decision to separate India's electoral system by caste, in the year 1932?
questions.questionHtml: In which prison did Mahatma Gandhi go on a hunger strike in protest of the British Government's decision to separate India's electoral system by caste, in the year 1932?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Yerwada.Key Points

  • In Yerwada prison did Mahatma Gandhi go on a hunger strike in protest of the British Government's decision to separate India's electoral system by caste, in the year 1932.
  • The Poona Pact was signed on 24 September 1932 at Yerwada Central Jail in Pune.
  • The Pact was signed between Dr B.R Ambedkar and Mahatma Gandhi.
  • Mahatma Gandhi went on a hunger strike and objected to the provision of separate electorates for the Dalits at Yerwada Central Jail. 
  • This Pact ended the fast that Gandhi had undertaken in the jail to protest against British Prime Minister Ramsay Macdonald’s award of a separate electorate to the Depressed Classes.
  • It was signed during the time of Lord Willington.
  • The Poona Pact refers to the agreement signed in 1932 to provide the depressed classes with the reservation of the electoral seats in the British India Parliament.
  • It was signed by Madan Mohan Malviya on the behalf of Mahatma Gandhi and B.R. Ambedkar at Yerwada Central Jail in Pune.

questions.question: Mahatma Gandhi called a halt to the Non-Cooperation Movement after the Chauri Chaura incident. Where among the following places is Chauri Chaura located?
questions.questionHtml: Mahatma Gandhi called a halt to the Non-Cooperation Movement after the Chauri Chaura incident. Where among the following places is Chauri Chaura located?
questions.solution: The Chauri Chaura incident occurred in the Gorakhpur district of Uttar Pradesh on February 4, 1922. It was a violent clash that resulted in the deaths of 22 policemen, led by Bhagwan din Aihir. This incident prompted Mahatma Gandhi to halt the Non-Cooperation Movement, which he had initiated in 1920 to protest against the Rowlatt Act, the Jallianwala Bagh Massacre, and support the Khilafat Movement. The movement involved the boycott of British goods, resignation from government jobs, and refusal to pay taxes. Gandhi was imprisoned for six months after calling off the movement, which laid the groundwork for future national movements.

questions.question: Mahatma Gandhi abruptly called off the Non-Cooperation Movement when in ________ a crowd of peasants set fire to a police station in Chauri Chaura.
questions.questionHtml: Mahatma Gandhi abruptly called off the Non-Cooperation Movement when in ________ a crowd of peasants set fire to a police station in Chauri Chaura.
questions.solution: The Non-Cooperation Movement led by Mahatma Gandhi aimed at achieving independence from British rule. However, in February 1922, a violent incident in Chauri Chaura led to Gandhi calling off the movement. This incident served as a reminder of the importance of non-violence. Gandhi's decision was difficult but in the best interests of India.

questions.question: During India's independence movement, who was the only President of the Indian National Congress who resigned from the presidency even after being elected?
questions.questionHtml: During India's independence movement, who was the only President of the Indian National Congress who resigned from the presidency even after being elected?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is Subhash Chandra Bose.Key Points

  • During India's independence movement, Subhash Chandra Bose was the only President of the Indian National Congress who resigned from the presidency even after being elected.

Additional Information

  • The Indian National Congress (INC) chose Subhas Chandra Bose as its President in 1938.
  • In 1939, he ran for re-election to the party's presidency.
  • Gandhi was a strong supporter of Pattabhi Sitaramayya for President. Bose was re-elected as president of the INC, however, thanks to the support of radical factions inside the party.
  • Gandhi was dissatisfied with his re-election and claimed that Pattabhi Sitaramayya's failure was his own.
  • Thirteen members of the Congress Working Committee resigned in protest over Gandhi's suffering.
  • Several delegates who had previously supported Bose began to endorse Gandhi at this time.
  • Bose resigned from the presidency in 1939 because it was getting increasingly difficult for him to work as Congress President.
  • When Subhash Chandra Bose resigned from the Presidentship of the Indian National Congress, the seat was offered to Dr. Rajendra Prasad.
  • He became a member of the Indian National Congress in 1911 when the annual session was held in Calcutta.
  • Dr. Rajendra Prasad was elected as the permanent president of the Constituent Assembly on 11th December 1946.

questions.question: The Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms led to the enactment of the Government of India Act of:
questions.questionHtml: The Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms led to the enactment of the Government of India Act of:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is 1919Key Points

  • Background:
    • In 1918, Edwin Montagu, the Secretary of State, and Lord Chelmsford, the Viceroy, produced their scheme of constitutional reforms, known as the Montagu-Chelmsford (or Mont-Ford) Reforms, which led to the enactment of the Government of India Act of 1919.
    • Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms came into force in 1921.
    • The sole purpose of this Act was to ensure Indians of their representation in the Government.
    • The Act introduced reforms at the Central as well as Provincial levels of Government.

Additional Information

  • Salient Features of the Act Central Level Government:
  • Subjects:
    • ​The matters, which were of National importance or related to more than one province were governed at the central level, such as Foreign Affairs, Defence, Political Relations, Communication, Public Debt, Civil and Criminal Laws, Wire services, etc.
    • The Central Legislature was made more powerful and more representative by this Act.
  • Executive
  • ​Reforms in Legislature
  • Powers of Viceroy
  • Powers of Central Legislature
  • Restrictions on Central Legislature​

Important Points

  • Significance of the Act:
  • Awakening Among Indians:
    • Indians received secret information about the administration and became aware of their duties.
    • This instilled a sense of nationalism and awakening among Indians and they moved towards achieving the goal of Swaraj.
  • Expansion of Voting Rights:
    • Election areas expanded in India and people began to understand the importance of voting.
  • Self-Government in Provinces:
    • The Act led to the existence of provincial self-government in India.
    • The Act gave the people the power to administer and administrative pressure from the government was greatly reduced.
    • It prepared Indians to discharge responsibilities in the provincial administration.
